extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for authors of moral or didactic essays, focusing on style, audience, usefulness, and the practical habits of composition. Emphasizes clarity, revision, social tact, and perseverance rather than genius alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' public usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The author is not wholly useless, who provides innocent amusements for minds ... There are so many more instigations to evil, than incitements to good, that he who keeps men in a neutral state, may be justly considered as a benefactor to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books of morality may not instantly reform nations, but their influence is gradual and often imperceptible; even works read for amusement can seed ideas that later find a receptive moment. Anti-pattern: rejecting the project of writing because immediate, visible large-scale reform seems unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write accessibly (clarity over abstruseness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is often more successfully propagated by men of moderate abilities, who, adopting the opinions of others, have no care but to explain them clearly, than by subtle speculatists and curious searchers, who exact from their readers powers equal to their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clear exposition and accessibility over technical subtlety that demands exceptional reader effort. Example: a moderate writer explaining established opinions clearly may be more effective than a brilliant but obscure theorist. Anti-pattern: producing work that is brilliant but unnecessarily difficult for the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful attention to words, phrasing and sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, therefore, as well as things, claim the care of an author. ... that he will run from one end of Paris to the other, for an opportunity of reading a period to a nice ear; that he will change a sentence, because the sound of a letter was too often repeated: that he was often disquieted with doubts, about the propriety of a word which every body understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meticulous sentence-level revision is required: monitor diction, cadence, repetition and aural qualities; consult friends or sensitive readers on a period's effect. Anti-patterns: leaving awkward repetitions, indifferent phrasing, or neglecting the music of sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and write for readers' motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some read for style, and some for argument: one has little care about the sentiment, he observes only how it is expressed; another regards not the conclusion, but is diligent to mark how it is inferred: some read that they may embellish their conversation, or shine in dispute; some that they may not be detected in ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate varied reader motives (amusement, style appreciation, argument, reputation, curiosity) and shape parts of your work accordingly. Example: include clear arguments for those who read for reasoning, attractive phrasing for those who read for style. Anti-pattern: assuming a homogeneous readership or ignoring common reader motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and method in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is, for the most part, an effort of slow diligence and steady perseverance ... the mind which, while it considered it in the gross, imagined itself amply furnished with materials, finds sometimes an unexpected barrenness and vacuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect toil, blocks, and confused drafts; rely on steady work and revision rather than sudden inspiration. Anti-patterns: abandoning projects at first difficulty or relying solely on an initial burst of fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be useful within your powers (measure ambition to ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man can only form a just estimate of his own actions, by making his power the test of his performance ... It is not necessary that a man should forbear to write, till he has discovered some truth unknown before; he may be sufficiently useful, by only diversifying the surface of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess your contribution against your actual powers and aim to do well what is within reach — clarifying, repeating, and popularizing as valid contributions. Anti-pattern: dismissing modest projects because they are not grand discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social tact and prevailing taste to increase influence
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the notions and practices of mankind, is in some degree the duty of a social being; ... the external mode is to be in some measure regulated by the prevailing taste of the age in which we live; for he is certainly no friend to virtue, who neglects to give it any lawful attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt surface forms (manners, dress, style, conventional attractions) as lawful ornaments to make virtue or ideas attractive and retain readers; Nelson's elegance in manners and dress is offered as an example. Anti-pattern: affecting contempt for common forms to the point that it repels the audience you wish to influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unjustified singularity and arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularity is, I think, in its own nature universally and invariably displeasing ... he who differs from others without apparent advantage, ought not to be angry if his arrogance is punished with ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve eccentric departures from custom for cases with clear advantage (e.g., moral or religious principle); moderate minds should not adopt oddities merely to appear superior. Anti-pattern: performing singular affectations that yield no evident benefit and alienate readers.
